title: A cross-lingual analysis on the spread of misinformation using the case of Ivermectin as a treatment for Covid-19
screen_reason: Twitter retweet-network study of the false claim that Ivermectin treats Covid-19, in English and Japanese (Feb 2020 - Mar 2022; 2,094,388 English retweets across 698,484 users, 3,056,884 Japanese retweets across 259,151 users). The paper labels users pro-use ('misinformation spreaders') or anti-use from their observed retweet behaviour and reports the share of users so labelled (57% English, 55% Japanese). That is a share of actors who amplified a false claim, from platform data - a SHARING actor_share with an explicit denominator. Included, but with reservations recorded below: the labels are stance labels propagated through the network, not per-user verification that misinformation was shared, and the denominator quoted alongside the percentages in the text is not the denominator that produces them.

estimates.country: not stated; users defined by tweet language (English), worldwide
estimates.platform: Twitter (retweets collected via Twitter REST API v1.1)
estimates.measure_type: % of stance-labelled English-language users in the Ivermectin retweet network tagged as pro-use, i.e. misinformation spreaders
estimates.value_raw: 57 percent of English users were tagged as pro-use (280,713 users tagged as pro-use and 206,428 as anti-use, i.e. 280,713/487,141 = 57.6%)
estimates.denominator: 487,141 English-language Twitter users whose stance could be assigned (280,713 pro-use + 206,428 anti-use), out of 698,484 unique users who retweeted content containing 'Ivermectin'; the labelling reached 69.7% population coverage in English
estimates.definition: a user tagged 'pro-use' ('misinformation spreader'): the top ten monthly influential users were manually tagged pro-use or anti-use from the sentiment of their tweets, then every connected user who retweeted pro-use users more often than anti-use users was tagged pro-use, propagated to six node hops
estimates.misinfo_def: the paper's target claim is that 'Ivermectin is an effective treatment for Covid-19'; no formal definition of misinformation is given, but the claim is treated as false because 'none have been able to convincingly show this in Randomised Controlled Trials' and the WHO and FDA 'continue to discourage consumption to treat Covid-19'
estimates.source_quote: Of the 698,484 unique users in English and 259,151 in Japanese, 57 percent of English users were tagged as pro-use, and 55 percent in Japanese.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Cross-lingual misinformation', p. 3; Methods, 'Cross-lingual analysis', p. 12
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two-stage actor labelling, not item verification. Stage 1 (manual): the top ten users by node degree in each month were manually reviewed and tagged pro-use or anti-use 'depending on the sentiment expressed in their tweets' (Tables 6-7); no coder count, no inter-rater reliability reported. Stage 2 (algorithmic): stance propagated to the rest of the retweet network by a majority rule - a user who retweeted pro-use users more times than anti-use users was tagged pro-use - repeated to six node hops in English and five in Japanese. Validation is informal: the authors cite the high proportion labelled anti-use despite a small anti-use seed, and the face validity of the top links shared by each group (Tables 8-9).
estimates.moderator_quote: The process was repeated to six node hops in English and five node hops in Japanese, achieving a population coverage of 69.7% in English, with 280,713 users tagged as pro-use and 206,428 as anti-use, and 82.6% population coverage in Japanese, with 118,474 users tagged as pro-use and 95,685 as anti-use.
estimates.notes: DENOMINATOR CORRECTION (adjudicator should see this): the sentence quoted introduces the 57% with 'Of the 698,484 unique users in English', but 280,713/698,484 = 40.2%, not 57%. The 57% is the pro-use share of the 487,141 users the propagation actually labelled (280,713/487,141 = 57.6%). I have kept the verbatim 57% and corrected the denominator; if the review prefers all network participants as the denominator, the R8-compliant alternative from verbatim counts is 280,713/698,484 = 40.2%, with the residual 30.3% of users unlabelled and of unknown stance. borderline=true because 'pro-use' is a STANCE label, propagated through the retweet graph, not a verified record that each user shared a false item: Table 8 shows the top URLs shared by English pro-use users include a Nobel Prize press release, a PMC review and a Reuters report alongside clearly false claims, so the numerator counts amplifiers of a pro-Ivermectin agenda rather than amplifiers of individually fact-checked falsehoods. breadth left blank because the classification is actor-level, as with source-level lists; the underlying claim ('Ivermectin is an effective Covid-19 treatment') would be 'false' if the review codes breadth from the target claim instead.

estimates.country: Japanese-language Twitter users; the paper treats them as the Japanese community
estimates.platform: Twitter (retweets collected via Twitter REST API v1.1)
estimates.measure_type: % of stance-labelled Japanese-language users in the Ivermectin retweet network tagged as pro-use, i.e. misinformation spreaders
estimates.value_raw: 55 percent in Japanese (118,474 users tagged as pro-use and 95,685 as anti-use, i.e. 118,474/214,159 = 55.3%)
estimates.denominator: 214,159 Japanese-language Twitter users whose stance could be assigned (118,474 pro-use + 95,685 anti-use), out of 259,151 unique users who retweeted content containing the Japanese equivalent of 'Ivermectin'; the labelling reached 82.6% population coverage in Japanese
estimates.definition: a user tagged 'pro-use' ('misinformation spreader'): manual stance tagging of the top ten monthly influential users, then majority-rule propagation through the retweet network to five node hops in Japanese
estimates.misinfo_def: the paper's target claim is that 'Ivermectin is an effective treatment for Covid-19', treated as false on the basis of RCT evidence and WHO/FDA guidance; no formal definition of misinformation is given
estimates.source_quote: Of the 698,484 unique users in English and 259,151 in Japanese, 57 percent of English users were tagged as pro-use, and 55 percent in Japanese.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Cross-lingual misinformation', p. 3; Methods, 'Cross-lingual analysis', p. 12
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two-stage actor labelling as the English row: manual stance tagging of the top ten monthly node-degree users from tweet sentiment, then majority-rule propagation to five node hops in Japanese, reaching 82.6% coverage. Keyword counting in Japanese used the spaCy and GiNZA NLP libraries. No inter-rater reliability reported for the manual seed.
estimates.moderator_quote: The process was repeated to six node hops in English and five node hops in Japanese, achieving a population coverage of 69.7% in English, with 280,713 users tagged as pro-use and 206,428 as anti-use, and 82.6% population coverage in Japanese, with 118,474 users tagged as pro-use and 95,685 as anti-use.
estimates.notes: Same denominator correction as the English row: 118,474/259,151 = 45.7%, not 55%; the 55% is the pro-use share of the 214,159 labelled users (118,474/214,159 = 55.3%). Country coded Japan because the sampling unit is the Japanese language and the paper frames the users throughout as the Japanese community and Japanese society; language is nevertheless not a country and a small share of these accounts may be outside Japan. borderline=true for the same stance-vs-verified-misinformation reason as the English row - Table 9's top pro-use URLs include mainstream outlets (Nikkei, Yomiuri, Asahi) reporting on Ivermectin alongside overtly false claims.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted: (1) population coverage of the labelling (69.7% English, 82.6% Japanese) - a methods completeness figure, not a misinformation share. (2) Retweet and user volumes (2,094,388 English retweets / 698,484 users; 3,056,884 Japanese retweets / 259,151 users) - denominators, not estimates. (3) Node-degree rankings, RBO similarity scores, monthly counts of pro- vs anti-use users among the top ten influential users (Fig. 2, Tables 2, 6, 7) - these are influence rankings, and the top-10 stance counts are a subgroup of ten hand-picked accounts per month, not a share of a population. (4) Retweet counts of individual top URLs (Tables 8-9, e.g. 7,389 and 16,136 retweets) - counts without a denominator. (5) Figures 3-5 (URL retweet-count scatter, non-native URL volumes, retweet timing distributions) are reported only graphically, with no numbers in the text. NO CONCENTRATION ROW: the paper is centrally about influential users, but it never states a 'top X% of users account for Y% of retweets' pair, so R1 (both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct required) cannot be satisfied - Fig. 4 shows the top 200 users by non-native URL count and their node degrees, without any share of activity. MAIN JUDGEMENT CALL: whether a propagated stance label ('pro-use') should count as observed misinformation sharing at all. If the review requires that the numerator's content be verified as false, both rows should be dropped or reclassified OTHER; I kept them because the labels are derived from real retweet behaviour towards a claim the paper establishes as false, and the paper itself glosses pro-use as 'misinformation spreaders'.

rob.design: Observational retweet-network analysis. Frame: all publicly available Twitter retweets containing the keyword 'Ivermectin' in English and its Japanese equivalent, Feb 2020 - Mar 2022, via the Twitter REST API v1.1; 2,094,388 retweets / 698,484 unique users in English and 3,056,884 retweets / 259,151 users in Japanese. No sampling within the keyword corpus and no response rate (platform census of the keyword). Exempt from IRB review as public data. Misinformation is operationalised at the ACTOR level: the ten highest-node-degree users per month per language were manually tagged pro-use or anti-use from the sentiment of their tweets (number of coders and reliability not reported), then stance was propagated through the retweet graph by a majority-of-retweets rule to six hops (English) and five hops (Japanese), covering 69.7% and 82.6% of users respectively. No fact-checking of individual tweets or URLs, no inter-rater reliability statistic, no held-out validation of the propagation rule; the authors offer only face-validity arguments. Keyword extraction used spaCy/GiNZA; network measures used networkx; rank similarity used RBO; retweet-timing data fitted with an asymmetric Laplace distribution.
rob.item6_quote: First, the top ten users for each month from the user influentiality analysis were manually reviewed and tagged as Ivermectin pro-use ("misinformation spreaders") or anti-use depending on the sentiment expressed in their tweets (Table 6 and 7). We then estimated the stance of remaining users to the next k-hops to get maximum coverage of connected users (Fig. 7). From the starting point of the manually tagged influential users, a given user who retweeted a pro-use user more times than an anti-use user was tagged as pro-use and vice versa.
rob.item10_quote: The process was repeated to six node hops in English and five node hops in Japanese, achieving a population coverage of 69.7% in English, with 280,713 users tagged as pro-use and 206,428 as anti-use, and 82.6% population coverage in Japanese, with 118,474 users tagged as pro-use and 95,685 as anti-use.
